old_entry.title: Dr. Mario
old_entry.subtitle: Dr. Mario Turns Falling Pieces into a Visual Diagnosis
old_entry.summary: On July 27, 1990 Nintendo takes Mario out of the platform game and places him beside a bottle full of viruses.
body: On July 27, 1990 Nintendo takes Mario out of the platform game and places him beside a bottle full of viruses. Dr. Mario keeps the immediacy of a falling-block puzzle but changes the problem with two-color capsules, fixed obstacles and a goal based on clearing the board rather than merely surviving. Its medical theme is playful, yet it makes color, risk and priority instantly readable. The result shows how a powerful character can cross genres without losing identity.

Dr. Mario is a falling block tile-matching video game. Mario assumes the role of a doctor, tossing two-colored medical capsules into a medicine bottle representing the playing field. This area is populated by viruses of three colors – red, yellow, and blue – which stay in their starting positions until removed. In a style similar to Tetris, the player manipulates each capsule as it vertically falls, able to move it left or right and rotate it 90 degrees clockwise or counter-clockwise.

When matching colors of capsule halves and viruses touch sequentially 4-in-a-row, they disappear. Any remaining half or whole capsules which are not supported will fall to the bottom of the playing field or until hitting another supported object, and any new 4-in-a-row alignments also disappear. The main objective is to eliminate all viruses from the playing field, finishing each level.

The options screen configures the starting level, game speed, and music. The player chooses a starting level between 0 and 20 that determines the number of viruses to clear, and one of three speeds of the falling capsules. The player's score is based on the elimination of viruses and the chosen game speed, with bonus points for clearing more than 1 in a single line. Dr. Mario offers a multiplayer gaming mode in which two players compete in separate playing fields. Each player's goal is to clear the private playing field of viruses first. Eliminating multiple viruses or initiating chain reactions can add capsules to the opponent's playing field. A player wins a single game upon eliminating all the viruses or upon the other player's bottle filling. The first player to win three games wins overall.

old_entry.title: Shadow of the Ninja
old_entry.subtitle: Shadow of the Ninja Turns Co-op into an Eight-Bit Choreography
old_entry.summary: On August 10, 1990 Natsume released Kage for Famicom in Japan, the game later known in the West as Shadow of the Ninja.
body: On August 10, 1990 Natsume released Kage for Famicom in Japan, the game later known in the West as Shadow of the Ninja. Hayate and Kaede can tackle stages together, combining platforming, combat and traps in a way that was unusual for NES action games. Katana attacks, chain weapons and acrobatic movement give rhythm to tight spaces where two players must avoid becoming obstacles to each other. Cooperation is not merely a social option here: it changes how the level is occupied and crossed.

Shadow of the Ninja is a side-scrolling platform game that can be played by up to two players simultaneously, with one player controlling Hayate (a ninja in purple) and the other as Kaede (a kunoichi in orange). In either mode, the player can decide which character they want to control before the game begins. There are no actual performance differences between either character. The player can run, crouch, climb ladders, attack, and jump like in most side-scrolling action games as well as hang onto an overhang and move under it. If the player has more than half of their vitality remaining, they can perform a special attack by holding a button for an extended period, summoning a thunderstorm that will damage all on-screen enemies, but at the cost of roughly half of their maximum vitality.

The player's default weapon is a katana, which can be traded for a kusarigama and vice versa. The kusarigama has a longer range than the katana and can be swung upwards diagonally and horizontally, but can only damage enemies from a specific distance and does not work as well at close range like the katana. If the player picks up a weapon they already have, its attack power will be strengthened by an increment of one level (with up to three attack levels). However, if the player takes too much damage, their weapon's strength will be reduced back to its previous level. There is also the possibility to use both weapons, if the player starts with the kusarigama and collects secret power-ups hidden in some levels. The player can also obtain throwable shuriken and hand grenades as well, both which can only be used as long as the player's supply lasts before the player reverts to using the katana or kusarigama. All four weapons are obtained by destroying item boxes scattered throughout each stage, along with vitality potions.

Shadow of the Ninja consists of five levels with fourteen stages, with the first four levels being divided into three stages and the final level into two. The player fights numerous types of enemy characters throughout each level, including bosses and sub-bosses. Once a boss has been defeated it will explode, this explosion will heal players the closer they are to it, since actually the same amount of health from one level will be carried to the next one until either recovered with potions or by dying. The game ends if the player loses all of their vitality and only five chances are provided to continue. If two players are playing the game, their continues will be shared.

old_entry.title: Super Nintendo Entertainment System
old_entry.subtitle: Super Famicom and the Super Nintendo family
old_entry.event_semantics: Scheduled published Playhub edition. The calendar slot is not asserted as a historical anniversary; the year is the source's historical anchor.
old_entry.summary: On November 21, 1990, Nintendo brings the Super Famicom to Japanese stores, successor to the Family Computer and the platform that would be known in the West as the Super Nintendo Entertainment System.
body: On November 21, 1990, Nintendo brings the Super Famicom to Japanese stores, successor to the Family Computer and the platform that would be known in the West as the Super Nintendo Entertainment System. The new machine does more than offer more memory, colors and sound capabilities: it introduces a controller with four face buttons and two shoulder buttons, expands the possibilities for moving backgrounds and makes it more natural to build games around depth, speed and transformation of space. Super Mario World and F-Zero, available at launch, immediately demonstrate two very different directions for the same technology. The historical value of the Super Famicom lies precisely here: hardware, peripheral and software are designed as parts of a single language destined to define an entire generation.

The Super Famicom controller retains the directional pad made familiar by the Famicom, but radically expands the number of actions immediately within reach. The four face buttons arranged in a diamond and, above all, the two L and R shoulder buttons allow commands to be distributed without forcing the player into constant combinations. This choice becomes important as games ask players to manage more functions at once, from running to combat techniques, rotation or quick selection. The controller is therefore not a neutral accessory: it anticipates the way increasingly complex genres will be designed. Nintendo would later describe how tightly the design of the console and its controls were intertwined. The physical shape of the peripheral thus becomes a concrete part of the generation's software language.

Super Mario World arrives with the Super Famicom on November 21, 1990 and works as a practical demonstration of the console's possibilities. The map connects levels into a continuous geography, secret exits alter the route, and Yoshi introduces a new relationship among movement, abilities and transformation of enemies. More colors and sprites matter, but the generational leap emerges above all from how those resources are organized. Levels can suggest more information without becoming unreadable, while animations and backgrounds support a greater variety of situations. Nintendo does not present technology as a list of specifications: it makes it understandable through a game that is immediately familiar but different enough to show what has changed. It is a launch strategy in which mascot, hardware and level design work together.

F-Zero, also available at the Japanese launch, demonstrates a possibility completely different from Super Mario World. The circuit is represented through the transformation of a large graphic plane that rotates and changes scale, a technique associated with the so-called Mode 7. It is not true polygonal geometry, but the effect produces a striking sense of speed and depth for a 1990 home console. The game's design grows around this capability: broad curves, readable obstacles and an elevated view let players interpret the track quickly as speed increases. The technical limit therefore becomes an aesthetic and mechanical choice. F-Zero shows how a hardware feature can become a recognizable genre and prepare the audience for a new way of perceiving space on screen.

The Super Famicom is often remembered as a 16-bit machine, but its technical identity is more interesting than a simple numerical label. Nintendo focuses on sprites, multiple background layers, scaling and rotation effects, a broader palette and a sound system capable of sampling. These characteristics favor games in which image and movement can become richer without abandoning two-dimensional logic. Nintendo interviews also reveal the other side of the equation: when Miyamoto and other developers want true polygonal objects, they discover that the console was not designed for that task. That very limitation leads to the search for additional solutions such as the Super FX chip. The machine's history is therefore also a history of production compromises, not abstract power.

For European players, the Super Nintendo arrived in 1992. The PAL machine kept the rounded outline and multicolour controller buttons associated with the Japanese Super Famicom, rather than the angular purple-button design sold in North America.

The controller expanded the familiar directional pad and face buttons with shoulder buttons under the player's index fingers. Stereo sound and richer imagery gave designers more room, but the results were not confined to spectacle. Super Mario World offered a colourful landscape of secrets; A Link to the Past built an adventure around revisiting places with new abilities; Super Metroid made exploration feel lonely and uncertain.

F-Zero and Super Mario Kart turned the new machine towards a different sensation: speed and competition. Looking across this library, the generational change becomes visible through contrasts. A single cartridge system could hold races, long journeys and quiet discoveries, each asking something different of the same controller.

old_entry.title: Commander Keen in Invasion of the Vorticons
old_entry.subtitle: Smooth scrolling brings platform games to the PC
old_entry.summary: On December 14, 1990, Apogee distributed the first episode of Commander Keen in Invasion of the Vorticons for MS-DOS through bulletin board systems.
body: On December 14, 1990, Apogee distributed the first episode of Commander Keen in Invasion of the Vorticons for MS-DOS through bulletin board systems. The project came from the group of programmers and artists who would shortly afterward found id Software, and demonstrated that the PC could deliver much smoother side-scrolling than was common in DOS games. Technology developed by John Carmack made it possible to move large portions of the screen without redrawing them entirely, bringing the immediacy of console platformers closer to the computer. Tom Hall built around that solution a child protagonist, levels full of secrets and a tone of animated science fiction. Apogee's shareware model completed the innovation: the first episode circulated freely, while the other two were purchased. Technology and distribution thus worked together to turn a technical experiment into a new studio.

At the beginning of the 1990s, the IBM-compatible PC was not the natural platform for a smoothly scrolling platform game. John Carmack developed a technique that moved the image by updating only the necessary parts of the screen, reducing the workload required from the system. That technical solution became the foundation on which Commander Keen could build jumps, platforms and side-scrolling routes with continuity closer to consoles. The historical point is not that the PC suddenly became identical to an NES, but that a limitation considered structural was bypassed through software and knowledge of the hardware. From that moment, the team could think differently about design. Technology stopped being a demonstration and became a language: it allowed Tom Hall to design larger levels, movement rhythm and secrets that depended precisely on the ability to scroll through space.

Tom Hall imagines Billy Blaze as a genius child who builds a spaceship from household objects and travels into space when his parents are not looking. This premise gives the game a tone different from heroic fantasy and from the more adult violence that would later characterize id Software. The pogo stick best summarizes the idea: it is not merely a gag, but changes height, inertia and the way platforms are read. Levels can hide optional routes, messages and secret rooms that reward curiosity and mastery of movement. Science fiction is filtered through a child's imagination, so planets and aliens can be threatening without losing their lightness. Commander Keen demonstrates that scrolling technology becomes memorable only when it meets a character and a set of rules capable of giving it an identity.

On December 14, 1990, Scott Miller began distributing the first episode of Commander Keen through bulletin board systems. The Apogee model used the software itself as advertising: a complete part of the experience could circulate freely, while players who wanted to continue purchased the later episodes. For a small team without a retail network, this structure reduced the cost of reaching an audience and allowed word of mouth to become commercial infrastructure. The first royalties convinced the group to leave Softdisk and, a few weeks later, formally establish id Software. The birth of the studio therefore cannot be separated from the way the game was distributed. Commander Keen shows that innovation in video games does not mean only inventing a graphics technique or mechanic: it also means finding a channel that allows that solution to travel far enough to support the people who created it.
